newsitem.title: SPAIN: SOCCER-SANZ AND GIL THE HEAVYWEIGHTS IN MADRID DERBY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SANZ AND GIL THE HEAVYWEIGHTS IN MADRID DERBY.

text.p: Two of the biggest heavyweights in the Spanish game have taken centre-stage ahead of Saturday's vital Madrid derby, but neither will be on the field.
While Real Madrid president Lorenzo Sanz hopes to see his side clinch their 27th championship, Atletico's Jesus Gil will take refuge from the possible celebrations in his country house.
Not that Gil's absence has stopped him warming up for the occasion in his own, inimitable style.
"You're nervous, you've got the nerves and contractions of a first-time mother," said Gil.
The remark was an opening salvo in a good-natured sparring match between the two men.
"We're going to be champions, and we'll baptise the child right there," replied Sanz.
"What's more Jesus, you're 64 now, and you won't see your next title 'till you use a walking stick," he added.
Sanz also jibed that he would invite Gil to take a dip in the Cibeles fountain, where Real fans traditionally celebrate.
"But there might not be any water left," joked Sanz, himself no lightweight, in reference to the corpulence of his opposite number.
Even if Gil were inclined to take up the challenge, he would find himself barred by railings designed to prevent the kind of damage caused in Real's last title triumph, two years ago.
But Gil is hoping the midnight swims will actually take place at the Neptune statue, where Atletico fans traditionally congregate after big wins.
The jovial atmosphere that exists between two men who are still clearly fans above all else perhaps reflects their humble origins.
Both are self-made men who have known how to ride the fickle wave of the Spanish construction boom.
Sanz began his career cleaning up in a barber's shop, and once sold water outside the Real stadium.
He now owns several companies, 70 racehorses and eight cars.

Gil, who gave centre-stage in last year's League and Cup double celebrations to his own prize racehorse 'Imperioso', juggles his financial interests with the responsibilities of being mayor of the resort town of Marbella.
Fans could be forgiven for thinking the presidents have turned their clubs into family businesses.
No fewer than five of Gil's relations are on the Atletico board, while one of Sanz's sons is a reserve defender for the Real side, and another plays for the club's basketball team.
But Sanz is quick to reject any suggestion of nepotism in team selection, saying that his sons actually find it more difficult to get picked at Real.
As if to prove him right, another footballing son has now moved on to Racing Santander.
Critics might suggest that Gil has had to resort to using his family because paid employees were fed up with his hire-and-fire style.
Staff at the Atletico club say they can't remember when asked how many coaches have come and gone in Gil's ten season at the Vicente Calderon, but the count is certainly over 20.
Atletico's first-ever double helped Radomir Antic find the soft spot in Gil, who says the Serbian can stay at the club as long as he wants.
But Gil's wilder side is still by no means tamed.

Last year he engaged in an ugly fist-fight with Compostela president Jose Maria Caneda. And in the past few days he has once again crossed swords with the Spanish Football Federation, who look set to take exemplary action.
